title: Seth Trimble, after 4-year UNC career and NBA Summer League stint, joins ACC rival Louisville
content:
Former North Carolina guard Seth Trimble — a four-year Tar Heel and two-year starter — has committed to Louisville, he told ESPN on Wednesday, making him the latest player from the recruiting class of 2022 to attempt to return to school.

Trimble, 22, seemingly wrapped up his UNC career in March and played for the Washington Wizards in the NBA Summer League last month, but he also entered the transfer portal in the spring. When the NCAA announced its new age-based eligibility rules earlier this summer, allowing current and future classes of athletes to play five seasons of college sports in a five-year window, the governing body opted not to include recently graduated players like Trimble from the 2022 class. But a growing number of former college players from the 2022 class have sued — in Ohio, Tennessee, California and Colorado, among others — for a fifth season of eligibility, with college basketball offering a more lucrative payday than options in the G League or overseas.

On July 31, a U.S. District Court judge in Colorado granted a preliminary injunction that gives the players from the 2022 class another year of eligibility for the coming school year, opening the door for a player like Trimble to return. The NCAA has appealed the ruling and said Tuesday it did not plan to issue a blanket waiver for members of the 2022 class to return under the new eligibility rules, but the injunction currently remains in effect.

Trimble, who averaged 14 points, 3.8 rebounds and 3 assists as a senior at UNC last season, is not a party to any of the state-specific lawsuits and is (at least presently) relying on the Colorado ruling for his additional year of eligibility. A source familiar with Trimble’s situation, who spoke anonymously because they were not authorized to speak publicly, said Trimble hadn’t signed an Exhibit 10 NBA contract, contrary to some public reporting, which would have been a potential other holdup for the NCAA from an eligibility perspective.

And because Trimble entered the transfer portal while it was open in April, he was able to transfer from UNC without further court intervention.

He chose to join Louisville, which already had one of the best transfer portal classes in the sport on paper.

Louisville had already signed four top-100 transfers, per The Athletic’s rankings: former Kansas center Flory Bidunga (No. 1), former Oregon guard Jackson Shelstad (No. 9), former Iowa forward Alvaro Folgueiras (No. 47) and former Arkansas wing Karter Knox (No. 89). The Cards also signed former Dayton guard De’Shayne Montgomery and five-star center Obinna Ekezie Jr., who reclassified from the high school ranks to join UL a season early.

Louisville landed at No. 11 in The Athletic’s most recent top-25, but with Trimble, the Cards should be in the preseason top 10 and on the shortlist of legitimate national title contenders.

Trimble played in 126 games over four years in Chapel Hill, and built a UNC legacy in the process. He was former head coach Hubert Davis’ only four-year player, and he also hit one of the most dramatic shots in the history of the UNC-Duke rivalry earlier this year: a buzzer-beating 3-pointer to upset the eventual No. 1 seed in the NCAA Tournament.

Davis said after that game that Trimble was “deserving of being remembered forever.” While he’ll now potentially play against UNC, Trimble said on social media Tuesday that he will “continue to represent this university for the rest of my life.”

Trimble said he explored a return to the Tar Heels, but ultimately decided to transfer because of a roster crunch in the backcourt.

“Know that the love I have for this place is irreplaceable,” Trimble wrote.

Trimble should immediately slot into Louisville’s new starting backcourt next to Shelstad, giving coach Pat Kelsey one of the more experienced guard tandems in the entire sport. At 6-foot-3 and 192 pounds, Trimble is an elite point of attack defender — which UL has largely lacked under Kelsey — as well as a solid slashing scorer. He never developed into much of a reliable 3-point shooter in Chapel Hill, with a career 29.4 percent from deep, but he otherwise checks just about every box the Cards could ask for in such a late addition.
